about.title: Function Notation: Reading and Using f(x)
about.length_note: About 30 minutes, a normal half-hour class. There are four small ideas (what f(x) means, evaluating, finding x for a given f(x), and meaning in context). Each one gets an example and a check question. Pause whenever you need to, because every beat stands on its own.

sources.title: Standards: Understand the concept of a function and use function notation (CCSS.Math.Content.HSF-IF.A)
3.1 Functions and Function Notation (College Algebra with Corequisite Support)

say.text: Welcome! Today we learn a short way to write a function. We'll go one small step at a time.
First, a reminder from last class. A function gives exactly one output for each input.
Here is the new way to write it: f(x). We say it out loud as "f of x".
It has three parts. f is the name of the function. x is the input. f(x) is the output that comes back.

show.text: f | the name of the function || x | the input || f(x) | the output

say.text: Watch out: in f(3), the parentheses do not mean times. It means "put 3 in as the input".

show.text: f(3) = the output when the input is 3

ask.q: How do you read f(3) out loud?
ask.why: f(3) is read "f of 3". The parentheses hold the input. They do not mean multiply.

say.text: f is only a name. We often use f, g or h, but other letters work too, like W for a function about weight.
You already know equations like y = 4x − 5. In function notation we can write the same rule as f(x) = 4x − 5.
Now the first skill. Evaluating means finding f(x) for a given x. Swap the number in for x, then work it out.

show.text: Evaluate = put the number in for x

say.text: Example: f(x) = 4x − 5. Find f(2). Put 2 in for x: 4·2 − 5. That is 8 − 5, which is 3.
Your turn, same function: f(x) = 4x − 5. What is f(3)?

ask.why: Put 3 in for x: 4·3 − 5 = 12 − 5 = 7. 12 forgets the − 5. 2 adds 4 + 3 instead of multiplying. 3 is the answer for f(2), not f(3).

say.text: Inputs can be negative or zero too. Put a negative input in brackets so the sign doesn't get lost. Take f(x) = 2x − 5.
Let's try one with a negative input. Take your time.

ask.why: Put −1 in brackets: 2(−1) − 5 = −2 − 5 = −7. −3 happens if the negative sign gets dropped. −5 is f(0).

say.text: Now a real-world one. In a game you start with 20 points and earn 5 points per level. Let g(n) be your points after n levels: g(n) = 20 + 5n.
Evaluate g(4): 20 + 5·4 = 40. In words: after 4 levels, you have 40 points. The input is levels and the output is points.

show.text: g(4) = 40 | After 4 levels, you have 40 points

say.text: Reading a statement like this back in plain words is called interpreting it in context. Let's practise.

ask.q: In the game, what does g(10) = 70 mean?
wrong: The function g is multiplied by 10 to get 70.
ask.why: The number inside the parentheses is the input (levels). The number after the equals sign is the output (points). Here, 10 levels gives 70 points.

say.text: The second skill goes the other way. Sometimes you know the output and want the input. Then set the formula equal to that output and solve.

show.text: Know the output? Set the formula equal to it and solve.

say.text: Example: f(x) = 2x − 5. Find x so that f(x) = 11. Write 2x − 5 = 11. Add 5: 2x = 16. Divide by 2: x = 8.
Now in the game. g(n) = 20 + 5n. How many levels gives exactly 45 points?

ask.q: For g(n) = 20 + 5n, which n makes g(n) = 45?
ask.why: Solve 20 + 5n = 45. Subtract 20: 5n = 25. Divide by 5: n = 5. Check: 20 + 25 = 45. 9 skips the 20.

say.text: Let's keep the two skills apart. Evaluate: you know the input and find the output. Solve: you know the output and find the input.

show.text: Evaluate: f(5) = ? | input known, find output || Solve: f(x) = 17 | output known, find input

ask.q: In the statement f(5) = 17, which number is the output?
ask.why: The 5 inside the parentheses is the input. The 17 after the equals sign is the output.

say.text: One more story, with money. A gift card has $120. A streaming plan takes $15 each week. The balance after w weeks is B(w) = 120 − 15w.
Evaluate: B(3) = 120 − 45 = 75. After 3 weeks, $75 is left. Solve: B(w) = 30 means 120 − 15w = 30. So −15w = −90 and w = 6.

show.text: B(3) = 75: after 3 weeks, $75 is left || B(w) = 30 → w = 6: after 6 weeks, $30 is left

ask.right: After how many weeks is $30 left on the card?
wrong: How much money is left after 30 weeks?
How many dollars does each week cost?
What is the balance after 3 weeks?
ask.why: 30 is the output, and the output here is dollars left. So we are looking for the input, which is the number of weeks.

say.text: One last idea. Inputs have to be in the function's domain, meaning the inputs that make sense. For B, w = 10 gives −$30, which is not a real balance.

ask.q: Which input would NOT make sense for B(w) = 120 − 15w, if the balance can't go below $0?
ask.why: B(10) = −30, which is below zero. B(0) = 120, B(4) = 60 and B(8) = 0 all work.

say.text: A heads-up for later. With lines you get one answer when you solve. With curved graphs, different inputs can give the same output, so there can be more than one.

show.text: Lines: one answer. Curves: sometimes more than one.

say.text: Great work. Here is today in four lines.

show.text: f(x) is read "f of x": the output for input x || Evaluate: put the number in for x || Solve: set the formula equal to the output || In a story, say what the input and output mean

say.text: Final check. Read it carefully: is it asking you to evaluate or to solve?

ask.q: If f(x) = 3x + 1 and f(x) = 10, what is x?
ask.why: 10 is the output, so solve 3x + 1 = 10. Subtract 1: 3x = 9. Divide by 3: x = 3. 31 is what you get by putting 10 in as the input. 13 is f(4).

other_side.claim: f is the name of the function, and f(x) is the output for the input x.
other_side.other_view: In everyday teaching, people often loosely say "the function f(x) = 4x − 5", and that is fine in this course. Higher-level math keeps a firmer line between the function f, which is a rule, and the output y it gives for an input. Both ways of speaking are common, so expect to see both.
